references.text: Elisha asks the Lord to strike the Arameans with blindness (סַנְוֵרִים), the same rare Hebrew word used for the blindness that struck the men of Sodom.
Blindness is mentioned as a curse from the Lord, where those afflicted grope and cannot find their way—parallel to the men of Sodom who could not find the door.
Paul strikes the sorcerer Elymas with temporary blindness as God's judgment, in a similar manner to how the angels struck the men of Sodom with blindness.
The context of the event: the two angels arrive in Sodom and Lot welcomes them into his house, leading to a confrontation with the men of the city.
The Lord inflicts spiritual blindness so that people see but do not understand—a broader biblical theme about blindness as God's judgment.
Genesis 19:11 is a concrete historical example of the principle in Psalm 94:23 that God's judgment strikes the unjust in their own actions.
The event in Genesis 19:11 illustrates concretely how God saves the righteous from the wicked, as promised in Psalm 37:40.
The blindness in Genesis 19:11 is a concrete fulfillment of God's help from heaven to humble the persecutor, as described in Psalm 57:4.
